title: GPR Alpha — Noise Regularization and the Bias-Variance Trade-off
description: An 80-point experimental dataset with significant measurement noise (σ ≈ 0.25, signal-to-noise ratio ≈ 4:1) demonstrates what happens when GPR's alpha parameter is set too low (model chases noise — CV scores become wildly unstable) or too high (model over-smooths — R² falls steadily). The cross-validation R² mean ± std display in the results panel is the primary diagnostic tool. You will sweep alpha manually, read the CV stability signal, then compare against auto-tune.

steps.instruction: The dataset has 2 inputs (x1, x2) in [0, 4] and 1 output (y). It represents experimental sensor measurements with σ ≈ 0.25 instrument noise on a smooth underlying response — about 26% noise-to-signal ratio. This level of noise is typical of physical test data (strain gauges, thermocouples, pressure transducers). Outlier rows have been removed by the Clean step, but per-measurement noise remains in every row and cannot be cleaned out.

quiz.question: The data cleaning step (Step 4 — Clean) removes outlier rows using IQR-based detection. After cleaning, each row still has ≈ 0.25 units of measurement noise. Why can data cleaning not remove this noise?
options: Cleaning tools do not work on datasets with more than 50 rows

Outlier detection finds anomalous rows — data points that deviate far from their neighbours. Measurement noise is a small, consistent variation in every row that looks indistinguishable from normal data at the row level. There is no single noisy row to remove; the noise is spread uniformly across all observations
Cleaning would need to know the true noiseless value to remove noise, which is not available
Both B and C — cleaning can only identify rows, not reduce per-row measurement uncertainty
quiz.explanation: Outlier detection works by comparing each row to its statistical neighbourhood — a row is flagged if its output value is unusually far from the bulk of similar-input rows. Measurement noise of σ=0.25 shifts each row by a small random amount that looks entirely consistent with the local response variation. There is no threshold that separates 'noisy measurement' from 'normal observation' at the row level. The right tool for measurement noise is not cleaning — it is the alpha parameter in GPR, which tells the model how much per-observation uncertainty to expect.

steps.instruction: Designate x1 and x2 as inputs and y as the output.
Apply Min-Max normalization to x1 and x2. Note: normalization scales the inputs to [0, 1] — it does not change the noise level in y or remove measurement uncertainty.

Baseline — default alpha=0.1: Open Step 8 — Model, select GPR, RBF kernel, alpha=0.1, test split 0.2, 5-fold CV. Train. In the CV table, note the R² mean and the ± std. This is your baseline: mean ≈ 0.88, std ≈ 0.04. The std of 0.04 means scores vary by about ±0.04 across folds — moderate and acceptable.

quiz.question: With alpha=0.1, CV R² = 0.88 ± 0.04. The ± std means different folds score differently. What does a low CV std specifically tell you about the model?
options: The model has a high R² — std and mean are the same thing
The model performs consistently regardless of which subset of data it trains on — low CV std is evidence of stable generalisation, not overfitting to any particular noise pattern in the training data
The model has no measurement noise in its training data
Low CV std means the model will score 0.88 exactly on any new dataset
quiz.explanation: CV std measures consistency: if the model scores 0.92 on fold 1 and 0.84 on fold 5, std ≈ 0.04, indicating moderate variation. If it scores 0.95 on fold 1 and 0.40 on fold 5, std ≈ 0.20, indicating the model is highly sensitive to which specific noisy points it happened to see during training. Low std does not guarantee high accuracy — it guarantees repeatability. Both pieces of information (mean and std) are needed: a high mean with high std is dangerous (unstable); a high mean with low std is desirable.

steps.instruction: Overfit the noise — alpha=0.01: change alpha to 0.01 and retrain. CV R² mean will drop to ≈ 0.66 and std will spike to ≈ 0.20. Scores across folds now vary roughly from 0.46 to 0.86 — the model is chasing the noise pattern specific to each training fold. Open the residual plot: training residuals will be near zero (the model is interpolating through noise), but test residuals will be large and scattered.

quiz.question: With alpha=0.01, CV std spikes from 0.04 to 0.20. Some folds score 0.46, others 0.86. What is causing this dramatic instability?
options: The test split is too small with alpha=0.01

Alpha=0.01 tells GPR that each observation has only σ²=0.0001 noise — far below the true σ²=0.0625. The model interpolates tightly through noisy training points, memorising each noise artefact. When tested on a different fold with a different noise realisation, the memorised artefacts do not transfer. Folds where noise happened to be coherent score well; folds where it was inconsistent score poorly
Alpha controls the number of training iterations, so 0.01 means fewer iterations
RBF kernel does not work with alpha < 0.1
quiz.explanation: Alpha is the noise variance added to the diagonal of the GPR covariance matrix. A small alpha forces GPR to pass nearly exactly through every training point, including the noisy ones. The model learns the signal plus the specific noise realisation of the training fold. Cross-validation exposes this: each fold has a different noise realisation, so the 'memorised' model from one fold performs poorly on another. The CV std is the diagnostic signal — it rises sharply when the model is fitting below the true noise floor.

steps.instruction: Find the noise floor — alpha=0.3: change alpha to 0.3 and retrain. CV mean should hold at ≈ 0.89 while std drops to ≈ 0.02. Test R² stays near 0.92. Compare to the alpha=0.1 baseline: similar mean, lower std. Alpha=0.3 is near the true noise level (σ=0.25) — the model correctly stops trying to fit below the measurement uncertainty.

quiz.question: Alpha=0.3 gives CV mean ≈ 0.89 and std ≈ 0.02, compared to alpha=0.1 giving mean ≈ 0.88 and std ≈ 0.04. The test R² barely changes. What does this tell you about the true noise level in the data?
options: The true noise level is exactly alpha=0.3 because that is where R² is highest

The true noise level is approximately σ ≈ 0.25–0.30: alpha=0.3 matches it well enough that the model stops trying to fit below the noise floor (std drops to 0.02) without sacrificing accuracy (mean unchanged). At alpha=0.1, the model was slightly underestimating noise, creating mild instability. The stability improvement without accuracy loss is the fingerprint of hitting the noise floor
Alpha=0.3 is universally better than alpha=0.1 for all GPR models
Lower CV std always means higher R²
quiz.explanation: The optimal alpha is approximately equal to the true noise variance. When alpha ≈ σ_true², the model neither chases noise (alpha too low) nor discards signal (alpha too high). The signature of the noise floor is: CV std stabilises (stops dropping) and CV mean stops improving. Here the transition happens between alpha=0.1 and alpha=0.3. On real experimental data where σ_true is unknown, sweeping alpha and reading the CV std trend is how you empirically estimate the noise level.

steps.instruction: Over-smooth — alpha=1.0: change alpha to 1.0 and retrain. CV mean will drop to ≈ 0.85 and test R² to ≈ 0.90. The model is now too smooth — it is discounting real signal variation as noise. The residual plot will show systematic structure (the model is missing genuine response variation).

quiz.question: At alpha=1.0, CV std is low (≈ 0.03) but CV mean and test R² both fall compared to alpha=0.3. What is happening?
options: Alpha=1.0 causes numerical instability in the GPR solver

Alpha=1.0 tells GPR each observation has σ²=1.0 noise — four times the true noise level. The model discounts every training point too heavily, producing an overly smooth surface that misses real response variation. Low CV std confirms the model is not overfitting; falling mean R² confirms it is missing signal. This is the bias half of the bias-variance trade-off: the model is stable but systematically wrong
More data points are needed when alpha > 0.5
The RBF kernel is incompatible with alpha > 0.5
quiz.explanation: Over-regularisation (alpha too high) is the opposite failure mode from under-regularisation (alpha too low). At alpha=1.0 the model is told 'I expect ±1.0 noise on every measurement' — so it ignores small-scale response variation as noise artefacts. The result is a smooth but biased surface. CV std is low because the model is consistent (not memorising noise), but mean R² is lower because the smooth surface systematically misses the true response shape. The sweet spot is the alpha value where CV std has stabilised low AND CV mean is still high.

steps.instruction: Auto-tune: reset alpha to 0.1 (default), then click 'Auto-Tune →'. Auto-tune runs a grid search over alpha values (and kernel options) using cross-validation. Compare its selected alpha to your manual finding from steps 5–7. It should select alpha in the 0.2–0.4 range, confirming your manual sweep.

quiz.question: Auto-tune selects alpha ≈ 0.3 — matching your manual finding. What is the practical rule for setting alpha when you do not have time to sweep it manually?
options: Always use alpha=0.1 (the default) — it works for all datasets

Set alpha to your estimated measurement noise variance (σ²). For clean simulation data σ ≈ 0.01–0.05, use alpha=0.01–0.05. For experimental data with moderate noise σ ≈ 0.1–0.3, use alpha=0.1–0.3. If noise is unknown, start at alpha=0.1 and raise it until CV std stabilises — that point is your noise floor estimate
Use the highest alpha that keeps R² above 0.70
Alpha should equal the dataset noise-to-signal ratio expressed as a percentage
quiz.explanation: Alpha represents the expected per-observation noise variance σ². For clean simulation outputs (near-deterministic), very low alpha (0.01–0.05) is appropriate — the model should interpolate closely. For experimental measurements, alpha should match the instrument noise level. When noise is unknown, the CV std sweep is the empirical procedure: raise alpha until std stops falling (the noise floor), then confirm mean R² has not dropped significantly. Auto-tune automates this procedure over the defined grid — it is a time-saving tool, but understanding the sweep is essential for setting a sensible search grid and interpreting the result.
